A physical object used for display

check.question: What does it mean to be cynical?

To be confused by complex instructions

check.question: What is an esoteric topic?

examples: She came up with an ingenious way to keep the squirrels away from her bird feeder.

examples: She acted as the liaison between the neighborhood committee and the city council.
The actor served as a liaison between the charity and the local community centers.
word-teach:liaison.origin: It comes from the French word lier, meaning to bind or tie.

check.question: What is the primary role of a liaison?
options: To act as a bridge between two parties
To lead a group in a protest
check.why: A liaison helps people or groups communicate and work together.

examples: He decided to turn his hobby into a lucrative small business.
The film star signed a lucrative deal to be the face of the new perfume.
word-teach:lucrative.origin: It derives from the Latin word lucrum, which means profit or gain.

check.question: What does it mean if a venture is lucrative?
options: It makes a lot of money
check.why: Lucrative describes something that produces a significant financial profit.

examples: Rain has been my nemesis all summer long, ruining every picnic I plan.
In the new movie, the hero finally faces his long-time nemesis in a dramatic finale.
word-teach:nemesis.origin: It comes from the Greek goddess Nemesis, who represented divine retribution.

check.question: If you call someone your nemesis, what are they to you?
check.why: A nemesis is a persistent rival or someone who is seen as a major enemy.

examples: He was completely oblivious to the fact that everyone was hiding in the living room for his surprise party.
The star seemed oblivious to the cameras following her through the airport.
word-teach:oblivious.origin: It is derived from the Latin word oblivisci, meaning to forget.

check.question: What does it mean to be oblivious?
check.why: Oblivious means you are unaware or not paying attention to what is happening around you.

examples: The restaurant owner worried about the optics of closing early during the holiday season.
The politician was concerned about the optics of attending the expensive gala during a recession.
word-teach:optics.origin: It is derived from the Greek word optikos, related to sight or vision.

check.question: When someone discusses the optics of a situation, what are they focusing on?
options: The physical appearance of the setting
How the situation looks to the public
The technical lighting of the room
check.why: Optics refers to how an event or action is perceived by others.

The celebrity wore an ostentatious gown that grabbed everyone's attention on the red carpet.
word-teach:ostentatious.origin: It comes from the Latin word ostentare, meaning to display or show off.

check.question: What does it mean to be ostentatious?
options: To be very quiet and shy
To show off in a flashy way
check.why: Ostentatious describes someone or something that is designed to impress others by being showy.

mnemonic:ambivalent.hook: Think of being ambivalent like standing on a balance beam; you are leaning both ways at the same time and cannot decide which side to jump to.

mnemonic:cathartic.hook: Imagine a cat finally finding a giant ball of yarn to unspool after a stressful day. That pure release of tension is cathartic.

mnemonic:poignant.hook: The word poignant sounds like pointing; it is a moment so moving that it points directly at your heart and leaves a mark.

mnemonic:nostalgic.hook: Nostalgic sounds like no-stall-gic, as if you are stalling your walk to look back at an old photo and linger in the past for just a moment.

mnemonic:surreal.hook: Think of a surreal situation as a real scene painted by a squirrel; it looks like the world you know, but the details are just a bit too wild to be true.

mnemonic:polarizing.hook: Polarizing is like the North and South poles; everyone is pulled to one side or the other, leaving no room to stand in the middle.

mnemonic:authentic.hook: Authentic ends with tick, as in a checkmark; when something is genuine, you can confidently put a checkmark next to it.

mnemonic:vulnerable.hook: Vulnerable sounds like a thin layer that a nerve can reach through; it describes that moment when you have taken off your armor and are truly open.

mnemonic:nonchalant.hook: Picture a cat casually walking away from a dropped vase, entirely unbothered by the crash. Nonchalant sounds like non-chalet, picturing someone too relaxed to even step inside a cozy mountain cabin.

mnemonic:notorious.hook: Imagine a no-tori-ous shark that is so famous for biting surfboards that local surfers refuse to enter the water. It sounds like no stories are good enough to clear its bad reputation.

mnemonic:obsolete.hook: Think of an old typewriter sitting in a dusty attic, completely replaced by a modern laptop. It is so obsolete that even the spiders refuse to weave webs on it.

mnemonic:ominous.hook: Picture an o-minous dark cloud shaped like a giant question mark hovering right over your picnic basket. It gives you an evil omen that your sandwiches are doomed to get soggy.

mnemonic:opulent.hook: Imagine a living room so opulent that even the house cat wears a diamond collar. It sounds like o-plenty of luxury packed into every single square foot.

mnemonic:paradox.hook: Picture a pair of ducks wearing tiny running shoes racing each other in reverse. A paradox is just a pair of docs that defies all logic.

mnemonic:pensive.hook: Imagine someone staring so deeply into a cup of coffee that they look like they are writing poetry about the foam. Pensive sounds like pen is active, as if their mind is constantly writing deep thoughts.

mnemonic:perseverance.hook: Think of a person persistently serving a tennis ball over the net until their arm falls off. Perseverance means per-severing through every single hurdle until you win the match.

mnemonic:pervasive.hook: Think of a per-vase smell of flowers that spreads into every corner of the room. It is a pervasive scent that you simply cannot escape.

mnemonic:philanthropy.hook: Philanthropy sounds like Phil-a-trophy, a guy who wins an award for giving away his money. He knows that true charity is the greatest prize of all.

mnemonic:pivotal.hook: A pivotal moment is like a pivot in basketball. It is the key move where the entire game changes direction.

mnemonic:plausible.hook: Plausible sounds like applause-able. If a story is worthy of applause because it makes sense, then it is believable and plausible.

mnemonic:poised.hook: A dancer who is poised stays perfectly still like a statue before the music starts. They are calm, ready, and fully in control.

mnemonic:precarious.hook: Imagine a prayer carried on a precarious, thin wire. It is a dangerous situation that leaves you feeling very insecure.

mnemonic:prolific.hook: Think of a pro who is always lifting the weight of work with ease. A prolific writer or artist produces so much that they seem like a professional machine.

mnemonic:provocative.hook: A provocative comment is like a pro-vocal speaker who purposely stirs the pot. It is meant to get a strong reaction from everyone in the room.

mnemonic:prudent.hook: Think of a prudent person as someone who keeps their pru-dent (true dent) in a safe place. They are too sensible to risk losing their smile.

mnemonic:quirky.hook: A quirky friend is like a quick key; they might open a door in a strange way, but they always get you exactly where you need to go.

mnemonic:rapport.hook: You have a great rapport when you can finish each other's sentences, like two people rapping or chatting in perfect rhythm.

mnemonic:reciprocate.hook: Reciprocate starts like recipe. If you share a great secret recipe with a friend, they will likely reciprocate by sharing one of their own.

mnemonic:relentless.hook: A relentless person is like a re-lent-less borrower; they just keep coming back for more, no matter how many times you say you have nothing left to lend.

mnemonic:reminisce.hook: To reminisce is to re-mini-scene; you are replaying a tiny, happy scene from your past inside your mind.

mnemonic:resonate.hook: When an idea resonates, it sounds like a ringing bell that keeps vibrating in your mind. It hits the right note and stays there.

mnemonic:reticent.hook: A reticent person keeps their thoughts on a re-ti-cent, or a tight-cent, meaning they hold onto their coins of wisdom rather than spending them on talk.

mnemonic:rhetoric.hook: Think of rhetoric as a red-hot trick of language. It is a masterful way to persuade others using just the right words.

mnemonic:sanctimonious.hook: Imagine someone acting like a saint while secretly eating the cookies they told you not to touch. That person is being sanctimonious.

mnemonic:scrutiny.hook: Think of a screw that needs to be tightened because it is under scrutiny. Someone is looking at it very closely to ensure it is perfect.

mnemonic:skeptical.hook: If you are skeptical, you keep your skeptical side tucked away like a skeptic cat who is not sure if that treat is actually good.

mnemonic:spontaneous.hook: Think of a sponge that suddenly absorbs water without being asked. It happens in an instant because the action is spontaneous.

mnemonic:stoic.hook: Picture a stone statue in the rain. Even when the weather is miserable, the stoic statue never complains or frowns.

mnemonic:subtle.hook: The word subtle is itself subtle because the letter b is barely heard when you say it out loud. It hides in plain sight just like the meaning.

mnemonic:succinct.hook: If you are succinct, you suck the excess words right out of your sentence. You keep it brief and hit the point directly.

mnemonic:versatile.hook: Think of a person who is the very best at playing with all their tools. They are very-able to handle any task thrown their way.

mnemonic:vicarious.hook: Imagine you are watching a movie hero take a risk; your heart races as if you are the one there. You are living vicariously by feeling the excitement without taking the risk yourself.

mnemonic:volatile.hook: Imagine a price tag that is so volatile it flies up and down like a feather in a storm. It is so unstable that it is hard to keep track of where it will land.

mnemonic:whimsical.hook: Picture someone who follows their whimsy like a breeze, changing direction with a light heart. They are whimsical, drifting wherever their imagination leads.

mnemonic:wholesome.hook: Think of a meal that is whole and nourishing for the soul. It is wholesome because it leaves you feeling genuinely better than before.

mnemonic:zealous.hook: Picture someone so zealous about their hobby that they could sell it to anyone. They have such intense energy that they are practically glowing with passion.

mnemonic:laconic.hook: Imagine a person who uses so few words that their sentence is like a short, laconic lap around a track. They get to the point before you even blink.

mnemonic:benevolent.hook: Remember the word ben, which sounds like benefit, and think of someone who always wants to do good. A benevolent person is always searching for ways to benefit others.

mnemonic:bespoke.hook: Think of a suit that fits perfectly because it was be-spoken for by you alone. It is tailor-made just for your shape.

mnemonic:bittersweet.hook: Imagine biting into a piece of dark chocolate that is slightly bitter but still sweet. It represents those moments that leave you feeling happy yet a little sad.

mnemonic:coherent.hook: A coherent argument is like a train where every car is connected. If the links are strong, the whole message stays on track.

mnemonic:conscientious.hook: A conscientious person treats every task like a science experiment where they must be precise. They have a conscience that won't let them cut corners.

mnemonic:debacle.hook: A debacle is like a dinner party where the host accidentally sets the table on fire. Everything ends in a sudden, messy collapse.

mnemonic:defiant.hook: Think of a tiny kitten hissing at a large dog. The kitten is small, but its stance says it is not backing down.

mnemonic:euphoria.hook: Euphoria sounds like a symphony where every note hits the perfect high. It is that peak feeling when you are walking on air.

mnemonic:finesse.hook: Finesse is having the fine touch of a master chef who saves a dish with a pinch of seasoning at the exact right moment. It is about handling delicate situations with smooth grace.

mnemonic:frugal.hook: Think of a person who is frugal as being free of a gull, because they save every penny rather than buying unnecessary treats.

mnemonic:galvanize.hook: Visualize a gal in a van who is suddenly jolted into action by a lightning bolt, perfectly galvanized to start her engine.

mnemonic:grandiose.hook: A grandiose person acts like a grand eye, looking down on everyone else as if they were the only one worth seeing.

mnemonic:haphazard.hook: If your life is a haphazard mess, imagine a hat that is thrown half-heartedly across a room and lands in a pile of laundry.

mnemonic:hedonistic.hook: A hedonist is always at the head of the list for any event that promises pure pleasure and comfort.

mnemonic:impetus.hook: Think of an impetus as the invisible pet us that pushes us to move forward and take that first step.

mnemonic:incognito.hook: When a celebrity is incognito, they are in cog and toe, hiding their face and walking quietly to blend into the crowd.

mnemonic:ingenious.hook: An ingenious invention is so clever that it seems like a genius used an inner genie to make it happen.

mnemonic:instigate.hook: Think of a gate that swings open when you instigate, or stir up, action. Just imagine a tiny nudge on the gate that starts a whole chain of events.

mnemonic:lackadaisical.hook: Imagine someone lacking a daisy, or anything else, because they are too lazy to move. They are simply lackadaisical about everything on their to-do list.

mnemonic:liaison.hook: A liaison is a link between groups. Think of a person who is the 'lie-son' who holds the 'reason' together by connecting the two sides.

mnemonic:lucrative.hook: If a deal is lucrative, it is like a lucky rate of return. It is the kind of job that fills your piggy bank with gold.

mnemonic:nemesis.hook: A nemesis is your ultimate rival. Think of a 'new mess' that your enemy always creates just to ruin your perfectly organized day.

mnemonic:oblivious.hook: An oblivious person is living in a bubble, so they have no 'ob-view' of what is happening around them. They are completely unaware of the world outside.

mnemonic:optics.hook: Think of optics as the way people look through a lens at your actions. Good optics mean the public sees a clear, flattering image of your work.

mnemonic:ostentatious.hook: An ostentatious person wants to be seen like a star on a stage. They act so showy that they are constantly saying, 'Oh, stay and see me!'

mnemonic:palpable.hook: Think of a palpable pulse you can feel with your palm. When something is palpable, it is so obvious you can practically touch it.

mnemonic:persona.hook: A persona is like a personal character mask you wear at a party. It is the version of yourself you choose to show to the world.

mnemonic:platitude.hook: Imagine a flat attitude that has been used so often it has lost its shape. That is a platitude, a once-meaningful saying that is now just tired.

mnemonic:pretentious.hook: If someone is pretentious, they are pre-tending to be more important than they actually are. They use big words and fancy habits to impress you.

mnemonic:quaint.hook: Think of quaint as a cozy, quiet antique shop. It is a word used for old-fashioned charm that feels warm and pleasingly unusual.

mnemonic:reckoning.hook: A reckoning is like a final bill being placed on your table at a restaurant. It is the moment when you must settle the score for your previous actions.

mnemonic:reverie.hook: Reverie sounds like a river flowing gently through your mind. It is a soft state of daydreaming where your thoughts wander freely.

mnemonic:riveting.hook: Imagine your eyes are riveted like bolts to a screen because the story is so good. If something is riveting, it holds your attention firm and fast.

mnemonic:underwhelming.hook: Think of a 'thunder-whelming' event where you expected a roaring storm but instead got a light drizzle. It is a loud promise that fails to deliver any rain.

mnemonic:unapologetic.hook: Visualize someone wearing a 'you-no-apology' shirt. They refuse to say sorry because they believe their actions are perfectly fine.

mnemonic:understated.hook: Imagine an outfit that is 'under-stated' because it lets your personality do the talking. It is like a quiet room that feels perfectly elegant.

mnemonic:vindicate.hook: Think of a 'win-the-date' victory in court. Once you win the case, you are vindicated and your reputation is cleared.

mnemonic:vitriol.hook: Imagine a 'vile-troll' shouting insults from under a bridge. Their bitter words are pure vitriol.

mnemonic:wanderlust.hook: Think of a 'wonder-list' of places you dream of visiting. That inner itch to cross every item off is your wanderlust.

mnemonic:wistful.hook: Picture a 'wish-full' expression on someone looking out a rainy window. They have a heart full of yearning for something just out of reach.

mnemonic:kpi vs metric.hook: A metric is just a bead on a string, but a KPI is the gold bead that actually helps you win the game. All KPIs are metrics, but only the goal-getters make the cut.

mnemonic:time to value (ttv).hook: Think of TTV as a countdown clock for a hungry guest waiting for their appetizer. The faster you serve the first bite, the happier the guest.

mnemonic:dau / wau / mau.hook: Remember the sequence as a calendar dance: Daily is a quick step, Weekly is a steady rhythm, and Monthly is the long walk home.

mnemonic:stickiness (dau/mau).hook: Think of sticky users like a favorite pair of jeans you wear every single day. The higher the ratio, the more comfortable the habit.

mnemonic:feature adoption rate.hook: Think of this as counting how many guests actually taste the new dish at a party. It measures if your creation is a staple or just sitting on the shelf.

mnemonic:retention rate.hook: Retention is like a boomerang that keeps coming back to your hand. The more it returns, the stronger your connection.

mnemonic:churn rate.hook: Think of churn as a leaky bucket where every drop lost is a customer leaving. You want to patch those holes to keep your count high.

mnemonic:cohort.hook: A cohort is like a high school graduating class; even as years pass, you track how the whole group evolves together.

mnemonic:ltv / clv (customer lifetime va.hook: Think of lifetime value as a long-term friendship where you calculate the total joy shared over the years. It is about the full journey, not just the first meeting.

mnemonic:task success rate / time on tas.hook: Think of TET as a trip to the dentist: how long are you in the chair, did you survive the procedure, and did you leave with a cavity?

mnemonic:jtbd (jobs to be done).hook: Instead of profiling who the person is, imagine they are interviewing a product for a vacancy; they only care if it can get the job done.

mnemonic:design thinking / double diamon.hook: Think of the Double Diamond as a pair of lungs: you inhale to explore and open up, then exhale to focus and shrink down, twice.

mnemonic:user journey map.hook: A User Journey Map is your user's travel itinerary, detailing not just the flights they take, but how happy or frustrated they feel at every stop.

mnemonic:empathy map.hook: Remember the four quadrants as a person's inner and outer self: what they say and do is on the surface, while what they think and feel is deep down.

mnemonic:usability testing.hook: Usability testing is like watching a friend assemble IKEA furniture; you keep quiet and just observe where they get stuck.

mnemonic:a/b test.hook: Think of A/B testing as a coin toss for data: version A and version B step into the ring, and the winner is decided by the user's clicks.

mnemonic:information architecture (ia).hook: Information Architecture is the digital blueprint of a building; if the hallways and rooms aren't labeled clearly, your users will never find the kitchen.

mnemonic:saas.hook: Think of SaaS as a streaming service for business tools. You simply subscribe to keep the software flowing, just like your favorite TV shows.

mnemonic:plg (product-led growth).hook: PLG means the product is its own best salesperson. It does the heavy lifting by inviting users in to play before they ever pay.

mnemonic:freemium.hook: Freemium is the classic 'free sample' strategy. It offers a taste for free, then lets the premium features do the selling for the rest.

mnemonic:tam / sam / som.hook: Think of it as a Russian nesting doll: TAM is the whole world, SAM is your neighborhood, and SOM is the house you are currently knocking on.

mnemonic:value proposition / positioning.hook: Positioning is your unique parking spot in the user's mind. Your value proposition is the reason they choose to pull into your space instead of the competitor's.

mnemonic:moat / network effect.hook: A moat protects your castle, while a network effect is the drawbridge that grows wider and sturdier the more people walk across it.

mnemonic:flywheel.hook: A flywheel is like a heavy merry-go-round; it takes a hard push to start, but eventually, your own momentum keeps the ride spinning effortlessly.

mnemonic:aarrr (pirate metrics).hook: Remember AARRR like a pirate finding treasure: you hunt for users, unlock their potential, keep them on your ship, claim the gold, and recruit their friends.

design-extras:aha moment.wild: You experience an aha moment when you finally find that specific song or photograph you were searching for after using a new app for the first time. It is that satisfying feeling when the product suddenly makes sense and solves your problem.
design-extras:aha moment.interview: I focused the onboarding flow on getting users to their aha moment as quickly as possible so they immediately understood the product value.

design-extras:time to value (ttv).wild: You notice this when a sign-up process is so streamlined that you are performing your first task within seconds of opening the app. A short time to value makes the difference between staying and deleting the app.
design-extras:time to value (ttv).interview: By simplifying the initial setup steps, I was able to significantly reduce the time to value for our new users.

design-extras:dau / wau / mau.wild: These metrics represent the heartbeat of a community, showing how many unique individuals engage with an online forum or social platform each day, week, or month. Developers look at these numbers to understand the scale of active participation.
design-extras:dau / wau / mau.interview: I analyzed the DAU and MAU trends to identify which parts of the user journey were driving consistent engagement.

design-extras:stickiness (dau/mau).wild: You see this in action when a news app or social network becomes a part of your daily morning routine. High stickiness indicates that the app is successfully woven into the everyday habits of its users.
design-extras:stickiness (dau/mau).interview: I suggested adding a daily notification feature to improve our stickiness and encourage users to return to the platform more frequently.

design-extras:feature adoption rate.wild: This is evident when a platform displays a small prompt or highlight for a new tool that only a fraction of the total user base is currently utilizing. It helps designers see if people are actually finding and using the new functions available to them.
design-extras:feature adoption rate.interview: We monitored the feature adoption rate to determine if the new navigation bar was intuitive enough for our users.

design-extras:retention rate.wild: You might observe this when an app emails you after a month to ask if you are still enjoying the service. It measures how many people keep coming back instead of leaving after their first visit.
design-extras:retention rate.interview: I prioritized improving the dashboard experience because I wanted to boost our retention rate by making the product more useful over time.

design-extras:churn rate.wild: This is felt when a subscription service sends you a final reminder email before your account is officially closed. It tracks the number of people who decide the service no longer meets their needs.
design-extras:churn rate.interview: To decrease the churn rate, I conducted user research to find out why people were cancelling their subscriptions.

design-extras:cohort.wild: You encounter this when you are part of a group tracked based on the month you created your account. This allows researchers to compare how people who joined a year ago behave differently than those who signed up yesterday.
design-extras:cohort.interview: I compared the behavior of the latest cohort against previous groups to see if the new update improved long-term engagement.

design-extras:ltv / clv (customer lifeti.wild: You might see this when a subscription service offers loyalty rewards or tiered pricing designed to keep you engaged for years. It reflects the value a service places on keeping you as a long-term subscriber.
design-extras:ltv / clv (customer lifeti.interview: I focused on improving the onboarding flow to increase the LTV of our new users by encouraging them to explore premium features early on.

design-extras:mrr / arr.wild: You encounter this when you choose between monthly or yearly billing options on a streaming or software service. These choices help the service predict their revenue stability over time.
design-extras:mrr / arr.interview: My goal for this feature was to drive higher MRR by making it easier for users to upgrade to our annual plan.

design-extras:arpu.wild: You notice this when a free app introduces a new paid feature that encourages occasional users to spend a little more. It helps the business understand how much value they generate from every person using their platform.
design-extras:arpu.interview: I analyzed our current monetization touchpoints to see how we could boost ARPU without compromising the experience for our free users.

design-extras:expansion revenue.wild: You see this when a service suggests a bundle or a professional add-on while you are already logged into your account. It is a common strategy for providing more value to loyal users who already know the product.
design-extras:expansion revenue.interview: I proposed a new dashboard notification that suggests complementary tools to our existing customers, which helps us drive expansion revenue.

design-extras:gross margin / burn rate /.wild: You might notice these concepts reflected in how frequently an app introduces new features versus how often it pauses development to optimize existing ones. These internal metrics often dictate whether a team is in a growth phase or a lean maintenance phase.
design-extras:gross margin / burn rate /.interview: I balanced our design roadmap to prioritize high-impact features that improve efficiency, ensuring we manage our burn rate effectively while still delivering value.

design-extras:nps (net promoter score).wild: You encounter this when a pop-up asks you to rate how likely you are to recommend the service to a friend on a scale of zero to ten. It is a standard way for companies to gauge overall user sentiment and loyalty.
design-extras:nps (net promoter score).interview: After implementing the new navigation, I tracked the NPS to see if users felt more confident recommending the app to others.

design-extras:csat (customer satisfactio.wild: You often see this as a quick feedback prompt immediately after you finish a support chat or complete a purchase. It helps the company understand how well they handled that specific moment of your journey.
design-extras:csat (customer satisfactio.interview: I designed the post-checkout screen to be as frictionless as possible because we wanted to maintain a high CSAT score for that interaction.

design-extras:ces (customer effort score.wild: You might see this in a survey that asks you to agree or disagree with a statement about how easy it was to solve your problem today. It helps companies identify which parts of their process are causing unnecessary frustration.
design-extras:ces (customer effort score.interview: I prioritized simplifying the account recovery flow because our internal data showed a low CES, indicating that users were finding the process too difficult.

design-extras:a/b test.wild: You might notice an app button changing from blue to green one day to see if more people click it. This is a common way to compare two design variations.
design-extras:a/b test.interview: I ran an A/B test on the checkout page to determine which layout led to a higher conversion rate for new users.

design-extras:information architecture (.wild: When you open a shopping site and see a clear menu that categorizes clothes into shirts, pants, and shoes, you are seeing good organization. This structure helps you find what you need quickly.
design-extras:information architecture (.interview: I audited the site navigation to improve the information architecture, making it easier for users to locate specific help articles.

design-extras:user flow.wild: Think about the sequence of screens you see when signing up for a new account, from entering your email to setting a password. That specific path you follow is the user flow.
design-extras:user flow.interview: I mapped out the user flow for the sign-up process to identify and remove unnecessary steps that were causing drop-offs.

design-extras:wireframe vs prototype.wild: A wireframe is like a simple blueprint of a website page, while a prototype is like a working model you can actually tap and interact with. Both help designers check their ideas before building the final version.
design-extras:wireframe vs prototype.interview: I started with a low-fidelity wireframe to align on the layout before creating a high-fidelity prototype to test the interactions with users.

design-extras:fidelity.wild: You might see a rough, black-and-white sketch of an app idea early on, which is low fidelity. Later, you see the polished version with colors and images, which is high fidelity.
design-extras:fidelity.interview: I decided to keep the designs at a lower fidelity during the initial feedback phase to ensure we focused on the core functionality rather than the visuals.

design-extras:progressive disclosure.wild: Many advanced settings menus hide complex options behind a single button so the main screen stays clean. Only when you click that button do you see the full list of choices.
design-extras:progressive disclosure.interview: I implemented progressive disclosure in the settings dashboard to prevent users from feeling overwhelmed by too many options at once.

design-extras:affordance / signifier.wild: A button that looks raised or has a shadow signals that it can be pressed, which is a visual signifier. The fact that it actually triggers a function when pushed is its affordance.
design-extras:affordance / signifier.interview: I updated the button styling to add a clear signifier, which significantly improved the affordance of the primary call-to-action.

design-extras:information scent.wild: When you click a link and the next page title matches what you expected, that feeling of being on the right track is provided by information scent. It helps you stay confident as you navigate deep into a site.
design-extras:information scent.interview: I improved the labels on our navigation menu to provide a stronger information scent, which helped users find their way to the account settings more quickly.

design-extras:feature flag.wild: You might see a new layout appear in your favorite shopping app only for a few users at a time. This is often controlled by a feature flag that enables the design for specific groups without needing a full app update.
design-extras:feature flag.interview: I utilize feature flags to roll out new designs to a subset of users, allowing me to observe performance metrics before a full release.

design-extras:scope creep.wild: A simple photo editing app that suddenly adds messaging, social feeds, and cloud storage might feel bloated and confusing. This is a common sign of scope creep where the original purpose of the app is lost to too many new requirements.
design-extras:scope creep.interview: To prevent scope creep during the design phase, I maintain a clear focus on the core user problem and push back on secondary requests that do not align with our primary goals.

design-extras:okrs (objectives & key res.wild: When a fitness app adds a new meditation tracker, it is likely tied to a company goal to increase daily active engagement. These goals are tracked through specific metrics that show if the new feature is actually working.
design-extras:okrs (objectives & key res.interview: I align my design decisions with team OKRs to ensure that every interaction I build contributes directly to our measurable success metrics.

design-extras:prioritization (rice / mos.wild: You might notice that a streaming service focuses on fixing search bugs rather than adding new social features. This is the result of teams using prioritization frameworks to decide which tasks provide the most value to users first.
design-extras:prioritization (rice / mos.interview: I use the RICE framework to prioritize design tasks by balancing the potential user impact against the development effort required.

design-extras:discovery vs delivery (dua.wild: A travel app might ask for your feedback on a new itinerary layout while simultaneously building the final version of the booking page. This split approach allows them to research new ideas while keeping the current product running smoothly.
design-extras:discovery vs delivery (dua.interview: I prefer a dual-track process because it allows me to conduct user discovery sessions while the engineering team completes the delivery of previously validated features.

design-extras:product-market fit (pmf).wild: When a small messaging app suddenly becomes essential for every student on campus, it is clear that they have found a strong demand for their service. This organic growth is a classic sign that the product has achieved a good market fit.
design-extras:product-market fit (pmf).interview: I look for signals of product-market fit by analyzing how naturally users integrate our solution into their daily routines.

design-extras:go-to-market (gtm).wild: Before a new ride-sharing service launches in a city, you might see advertisements and special discount codes appear everywhere. This coordinated effort is part of their strategy to introduce the product and gain new customers.
design-extras:go-to-market (gtm).interview: I collaborate closely with marketing and sales to ensure our design reflects the overarching go-to-market strategy for the product launch.

design-extras:prd (product requirements.wild: While you never see this document, it is the blueprint that guides the development of the apps you use every day. It ensures that everyone on the team understands exactly what functionality is being built and why.
design-extras:prd (product requirements.interview: I start by drafting a comprehensive PRD to ensure the design requirements and user goals are clearly communicated to all stakeholders before we begin prototyping.

design-extras:stakeholder.wild: You might notice a project timeline changing because a project manager or a lead engineer requests a new feature. These different groups represent the people who care about how the final product performs.
design-extras:stakeholder.interview: I ensure I align with every stakeholder early in the discovery phase to understand their specific needs and constraints.

design-extras:b2b / b2c / b2b2c / d2c.wild: You can identify these models by looking at who the website is intended for, such as a professional dashboard for office teams or a simple storefront for individual shoppers. These distinctions guide how the service is priced and marketed to the end user.
design-extras:b2b / b2c / b2b2c / d2c.interview: I tailored the onboarding flow to address the specific pain points of a B2B audience who needs to manage complex team permissions.

design-extras:saas.wild: You see this model when you sign up for a monthly plan to access a cloud-based photo editor or a project tracking tool in your browser. It allows you to use the latest version of the software without needing to install anything on your computer.
design-extras:saas.interview: In my previous role, I focused on reducing churn in our SaaS platform by streamlining the account upgrade process.

design-extras:plg (product-led growth).wild: You encounter this when you start using a free version of a drawing app and find it so useful that you decide to invite your colleagues to join. The tool naturally spreads through word-of-mouth as more people start using it for their own work.
design-extras:plg (product-led growth).interview: I designed the invitation workflow to support a PLG strategy by making it effortless for current users to bring their teammates into the workspace.

design-extras:freemium.wild: You see this when a music streaming app lets you listen for free with occasional advertisements or offers a paid subscription for an ad-free experience. It allows new users to try the service before deciding to pay for advanced features.
design-extras:freemium.interview: My design approach for the freemium model was to provide enough core utility to retain free users while clearly demonstrating the value of our paid tier.

design-extras:tam / sam / som.wild: You might read about these concepts in a business article discussing whether a new mobile game has the potential to reach millions of global players. It helps investors understand the potential scale of a product's reach.
design-extras:tam / sam / som.interview: When evaluating this product opportunity, I considered the TAM to ensure our design efforts were focused on a market with significant room for growth.

design-extras:value proposition / positi.wild: You notice this when a landing page clearly states exactly how the service makes your daily routine easier compared to other similar apps. It is the core message that tells you why you should choose this product over others.
design-extras:value proposition / positi.interview: I conducted user research to refine our value proposition so that the messaging would resonate more effectively with our primary user persona.

design-extras:moat / network effect.wild: You see this in social media platforms where the experience becomes much more engaging as more of your friends and colleagues join the community. This creates a strong barrier for competitors because users are unlikely to leave a platform where everyone they know is already active.
design-extras:moat / network effect.interview: I prioritized social sharing features to strengthen our network effect and increase the long-term defensibility of the product.

design-extras:circles.wild: When you encounter a new feature in a music streaming app that changes how you discover songs, you are seeing the result of a structured design process. Developers use systematic methods to ensure every change addresses a specific user need before it reaches your screen.
design-extras:circles.interview: I will use the CIRCLES framework to ensure I thoroughly understand the user needs and prioritize the most impactful solution for this design challenge.

design-extras:star.wild: When you read a user story or a case study about how a team solved a complex navigation problem, you are often seeing the STAR method in action. It helps teams clearly communicate how they turned a difficult challenge into a successful feature update.
design-extras:star.interview: Using the STAR method, I can walk you through how I identified a drop-off point in the onboarding flow and improved user retention by fifteen percent.

design-extras:double diamond.wild: You can see the Double Diamond process reflected in how apps evolve, starting from broad research into what people want, narrowing down to a core problem, and then iterating on the final design. It is the logical path from a messy idea to a polished, functional interface.
design-extras:double diamond.interview: I applied the Double Diamond process to this project by first discovering deep user pain points before narrowing my focus to define the primary solution.

design-extras:app critique approach.wild: When you find an app that is frustrating to use because the buttons are hard to find, you are noticing a failure in its design heuristics. A thoughtful critique looks at these small details to explain why a specific interaction feels intuitive or confusing.
design-extras:app critique approach.interview: To start this app critique, I will walk through the checkout flow and highlight where current UI patterns violate core usability heuristics.

design-extras:product sense round.wild: A product sense round is similar to looking at a popular social media app and asking why it remains successful despite constant changes to its layout. It is about understanding the strategy and user value behind the features you see every day.
design-extras:product sense round.interview: During this product sense round, I want to focus on the long-term goals of the platform and how we can best serve our power users through strategic feature updates.

examples: Her sense of style is truly impeccable, even when she is just running simple errands.
The film has been praised for its impeccable cinematography and haunting musical score.
word-teach:impeccable.origin: The word comes from the Latin word impeccabilis, meaning not capable of sin.

check.question: If a performance is described as impeccable, what does that mean?
check.why: Impeccable describes something that is perfect and free from any faults or errors.

examples: It is imperative that we leave for the airport now if we want to beat the traffic.
The director argued that it is imperative for the main character to show growth by the end of the story.
word-teach:imperative.origin: It originates from the Latin imperare, meaning to command.

check.question: What does it mean if something is imperative?
check.why: Imperative refers to something that is crucial or essential to do.

examples: There was an implicit understanding between them that they would meet at the cafe every Sunday.
The documentary carries an implicit message about the importance of protecting our natural resources.
word-teach:implicit.origin: The word comes from the Latin implicitus, meaning entangled or involved.

check.question: If an agreement is implicit, how is it communicated?
check.why: Implicit means something is understood or suggested without being explicitly stated.

examples: I am so sorry, that was a completely inadvertent mistake on my part.
The athlete made an inadvertent movement that resulted in a penalty during the final match.
word-teach:inadvertent.origin: It is derived from the Latin in- (not) and advertere (to turn the mind to).

check.question: What is an inadvertent action?
options: An action done with careful planning.
An action done to cause harm.
check.why: Inadvertent describes something done unintentionally or without conscious thought.

examples: The incessant rain meant we had to stay indoors for the entire weekend.
The reporter grew tired of the incessant questions about his personal life during the press tour.
word-teach:incessant.origin: It stems from the Latin incessans, meaning not ceasing.

check.question: How would you describe an incessant noise?
options: A noise that is very pleasant.
check.why: Incessant refers to something that continues without pause or interruption, often in an annoying way.

examples: With the storm clouds gathering, it felt inevitable that we would get caught in the rain.
The actor spoke about the inevitable changes that come with fame and global recognition.
word-teach:inevitable.origin: It comes from the Latin inevitabilis, meaning unavoidable.

check.question: If an event is inevitable, what does that mean?
options: It is highly unlikely to occur.
check.why: Inevitable describes something that is certain to happen and cannot be stopped.

examples: She seems to have an innate ability to make everyone around her feel comfortable.
Some believe that a sense of rhythm is an innate quality rather than a learned skill.
word-teach:innate.origin: It originates from the Latin innatus, meaning born in.

check.question: If a talent is innate, how did the person get it?
options: They bought it at a store.
check.why: Innate refers to qualities or abilities that are present from birth.

examples: The insidious nature of the illness meant it went unnoticed for several months.
The film explores the insidious influence of social media on our daily habits.
word-teach:insidious.origin: It comes from the Latin insidiosus, meaning deceitful or cunning.

check.question: Why is something described as insidious?
options: Because it is very loud and obvious.
Because it causes harm slowly and secretly.
Because it is meant to be funny.
check.why: Insidious describes something that is harmful but spreads in a gradual, stealthy, or deceptive way.

examples: I have been playing this game for so long that the controls feel completely intuitive now.
The actor gave an intuitive performance that felt like he was living the character rather than just reading lines.
word-teach:intuitive.origin: It originates from the late Latin word intuitus, meaning to look at or contemplate.

check.question: Which of these best describes an intuitive action?
options: Doing something based on instinct without needing to think.
Following a very strict set of written instructions.
Learning a new skill through intense academic study.
check.why: Intuitive means acting naturally or spontaneously without the need for conscious reasoning.

examples: After traveling for three months straight, I felt a bit jaded and just wanted to stay home.
The critic felt jaded by the endless stream of superhero movies flooding the cinema this summer.

check.question: If someone is jaded, how are they likely feeling?
options: Tired and cynical from too much of the same thing.
Eager to experience something for the very first time.
check.why: Being jaded usually implies that a person has lost their enthusiasm due to overexposure or exhaustion.

examples: The juxtaposition of the bright modern furniture against the old stone walls looked surprisingly good.
The film uses the juxtaposition of peaceful nature scenes and chaotic city life to highlight the main theme.
word-teach:juxtaposition.origin: It comes from the Latin word juxta, meaning near, combined with the word position.

check.question: What happens when you use juxtaposition?
options: You blend two things until they are identical.
You hide one thing behind another.
You place two different things together to highlight their contrast.
check.why: Juxtaposition is specifically used to show how things differ when they are put side by side.

examples: I felt so lethargic after the big lunch that I could barely keep my eyes open.
The athlete appeared lethargic during the second half of the match, showing none of his usual energy.
word-teach:lethargic.origin: It comes from the Greek word lethargos, meaning forgetful or inactive.

check.question: Which word is a synonym for lethargic?
check.why: Lethargic describes a state of low energy, slowness, or inactivity.

examples: She gave a very lucid explanation of how to fix the broken sink so I could do it myself.
The director provided a lucid account of her creative process during the interview.
word-teach:lucid.origin: It comes from the Latin word lucidus, which means bright or clear.

check.question: If an explanation is lucid, what is it like?
options: Very confusing and hard to follow.
Filled with too many technical terms.
check.why: A lucid explanation is one that is presented in a way that makes the message easy to grasp.

examples: Even though he lost the game, he was magnanimous enough to congratulate his opponent on a great performance.
The actress was magnanimous in her victory speech, thanking all the other nominees for their hard work.
word-teach:magnanimous.origin: It is derived from the Latin words magnus, meaning great, and animus, meaning soul or spirit.

check.question: What does it mean to be magnanimous?
options: To be stingy with your time or money.
To be noble and generous, especially toward a rival.
To be very competitive and focused on winning.
check.why: A magnanimous person shows greatness of spirit and kindness, often toward those they compete against.

examples: Watching the rain fall on a quiet afternoon often puts me in a state of soft melancholy.
The singer captured a sense of deep melancholy in her latest album, reflecting on her past experiences.
word-teach:melancholy.origin: It originates from the Greek words melas, meaning black, and chole, meaning bile.

check.question: Which feeling best describes melancholy?
check.why: Melancholy is a feeling of pensive sadness, often without a specific or immediate cause.

examples: We bought a fan to help mitigate the heat in our apartment during the summer.
The city is taking steps to mitigate the impact of the storm on the local neighborhoods.
word-teach:mitigate.origin: It comes from the Latin word mitigare, which means to soften.

check.question: If you mitigate a problem, what are you doing?
options: Reducing the severity of the problem.
check.why: To mitigate means to take action to lessen the harshness or negative effects of something.

examples: The pervasive smell of smoke from the nearby wildfire made it hard to stay outside for long.
The journalist noted that a pervasive sense of anxiety had settled over the city following the recent storm.
word-teach:pervasive.origin: It comes from the Latin word pervadere, meaning to go or spread through.

check.question: If a problem is pervasive, what does that mean?
options: It is very small and hard to find.
check.why: Pervasive describes something that permeates or affects every part of an area or situation.

examples: She decided to donate a portion of her savings to a local animal shelter as an act of personal philanthropy.
The actor is well known for his commitment to environmental philanthropy and support for global conservation efforts.
word-teach:philanthropy.origin: It is derived from the Greek words philos meaning loving and anthropos meaning human.

check.question: What is an example of philanthropy?
options: Donating money to help a local school.
Buying a new car for personal use.
Training for a professional sports team.
check.why: Philanthropy refers to the practice of giving money or resources to help others or support good causes.

examples: That was a pivotal moment in our road trip because we finally realized we had missed our exit.
The critic argued that this scene was pivotal to understanding the main character's true motivations.
word-teach:pivotal.origin: It comes from the French word pivot, referring to a pin or shaft on which something turns.

check.question: If an event is pivotal, how should you describe it?
options: It is very important and influential.
It is expected to happen again.
check.why: A pivotal moment is a turning point that has a significant impact on the outcome of events.

examples: It seems plausible that we could finish painting the living room by the end of the weekend.
The mystery film offers a plausible explanation for the disappearance that keeps the audience guessing until the end.
word-teach:plausible.origin: It originates from the Latin word plausibilis, meaning worthy of applause or acceptable.

check.question: Which of these is most plausible?
options: A cat learning to speak fluent French.
A person walking to the store to buy milk.
An elephant flying to the moon.
check.why: Plausible means something is reasonable, likely, or believable.

examples: We are all poised and ready to leave as soon as the taxi arrives.
The team is poised to make a major comeback in the second half of the championship game.
word-teach:poised.origin: It comes from the Old French word peiser, meaning to weigh.

check.question: If an athlete is poised for victory, what are they?
options: They are prepared and ready to win.
They have already lost the game.
They are resting after the event.
check.why: To be poised means to be fully prepared or in position for something to happen.

examples: The old ladder looked precarious, so I decided not to climb it to fix the light.
The mountain climber found himself in a precarious position halfway up the icy cliff.
word-teach:precarious.origin: It comes from the Latin word precarius, meaning obtained by prayer or dependent on the favor of others.

check.question: Which situation is precarious?
options: Sitting securely on a sturdy chair.
Balancing on a thin ledge over a deep hole.
check.why: Precarious describes a situation that is unstable or dangerous.

examples: My aunt is a prolific gardener who grows enough vegetables to share with the whole neighborhood.
The author is known as a prolific writer who releases a new mystery novel every single year.
word-teach:prolific.origin: It is derived from the Latin word proles, meaning offspring, combined with facere, meaning to make.

check.question: What does it mean to be a prolific artist?
options: You create a large amount of work.
You only paint in one specific color.
check.why: Prolific means producing a large quantity of something, such as art or writing.

examples: He made a provocative comment about the new film that started a long debate among his friends.
The documentary takes a provocative look at modern habits, challenging viewers to rethink their daily routines.
word-teach:provocative.origin: It comes from the Latin word provocare, meaning to call forth or challenge.

check.question: What is likely to happen after a provocative statement?
options: Everyone will agree with it immediately.
It will likely cause a strong reaction or argument.
check.why: Provocative things are intended to stir up strong feelings or reactions in others.

examples: I think we need to look past the political rhetoric and focus on what the candidate actually plans to do.
The film is filled with empty rhetoric about saving the world, but it lacks a compelling story to back it up.
word-teach:rhetoric.origin: It comes from the Greek word rhetorike, referring to the art of an orator.

check.question: What is rhetoric primarily used for?
check.why: Rhetoric is the study or art of using language effectively to influence or convince others.

examples: It felt quite sanctimonious of him to lecture me on healthy eating while he was eating a giant slice of cake.
The actor gave a sanctimonious speech about humility while showing off his expensive car in the same interview.
word-teach:sanctimonious.origin: It is derived from the Latin word sanctimonia, meaning holiness or sacredness.

check.question: If someone is being sanctimonious, how are they acting?
options: They are acting as if they are morally superior to everyone else.
They are being very quiet and reserved about their opinions.
They are openly admitting to their mistakes and flaws.
check.why: A sanctimonious person pretends to be more virtuous or pious than others, often in a hypocritical way.

examples: My travel plans are under close scrutiny because I am trying to stick to a very tight budget.
The athlete's performance has been under intense scrutiny since the start of the championship season.
word-teach:scrutiny.origin: It comes from the Latin word scrutari, which originally meant to sort through trash or search for something.

check.question: What does it mean to put something under scrutiny?
options: To hide it from public view
check.why: Scrutiny refers to a critical and thorough investigation or observation of someone or something.

examples: I am a bit skeptical about whether this new restaurant will actually stay open for long.
The film critic was skeptical of the director's attempt to turn such a famous book into a musical.
word-teach:skeptical.origin: It is derived from the Greek word skeptikos, meaning inquiring or reflective.

check.question: How does a skeptical person feel?
check.why: Being skeptical means you have reservations or doubts about the truth or validity of something.

examples: We decided to go on a spontaneous trip to the coast after seeing how sunny it was outside.
The singer's spontaneous decision to perform an acoustic set delighted the fans in the crowd.
word-teach:spontaneous.origin: It stems from the Latin word sponte, which means of one's own free will.

check.question: What is a spontaneous decision?
options: One that was planned for weeks
One made without any prior planning
One that is forced by someone else
check.why: Spontaneous actions happen naturally and suddenly without being forced or planned in advance.

examples: She remained stoic even when she received the disappointing news about her flight being cancelled.
The captain kept a stoic expression while the team suffered a crushing defeat in the final minutes.
word-teach:stoic.origin: It comes from the Stoa Poikile, a porch in Athens where early philosophers taught.

check.question: How does a stoic person behave during a difficult time?
options: They hide their pain and remain calm.
They panic and look for help.
check.why: A stoic person endures pain or hardship without showing their feelings or complaining.

examples: There was a subtle change in the lighting that made the whole room feel much warmer.
The actor gave a subtle performance that revealed the character's sadness without saying a word.
word-teach:subtle.origin: It comes from the Latin word subtilis, meaning fine, thin, or delicate.

check.question: What is something subtle?
options: Something that is very obvious and loud
Something that is hard to notice at first
Something that is completely impossible to see
check.why: Subtle things are delicate or indirect, making them not immediately or easily noticed.

examples: Please try to keep your explanation of the directions succinct so we can get going.
The reviewer gave a succinct summary of the movie that made me want to see it immediately.
word-teach:succinct.origin: It comes from the Latin word succingere, which means to tuck up or gather up.

check.question: What does it mean to be succinct?
options: To speak in a very long and detailed way
To speak clearly and using few words
To speak in a way that is hard to follow
check.why: Succinct speech or writing is brief, concise, and gets directly to the main point.

examples: I felt that our conversation was just too superficial to really get to know each other.
The film critic noted that the screenplay was superficial and lacked any real emotional depth.
word-teach:superficial.origin: The word comes from the Latin word superficialis, which means on the surface.

check.question: If someone describes a conversation as superficial, what do they mean?
options: It was very deep and personal.
check.why: Superficial refers to things that remain on the surface rather than exploring deeper meaning.

examples: She is a tenacious runner who never gives up even when the race gets difficult.
The documentary highlights the tenacious efforts of the explorer to reach the remote mountain peak.
word-teach:tenacious.origin: It originates from the Latin word tenax, meaning holding fast.

check.question: Which of these best describes a tenacious person?
options: Someone who prefers to work alone.
check.why: A tenacious person is someone who holds onto their goal and does not give up easily.

examples: We have a tentative plan to meet for coffee on Saturday, but it depends on the weather.
The band made a tentative announcement about a possible summer tour next year.
word-teach:tentative.origin: It comes from the Latin word tentare, which means to try or to test.

check.question: If a plan is described as tentative, what does that imply?
options: It is finalized and cannot change.
It is not yet definite and could change.
check.why: Tentative plans are uncertain and subject to change.

examples: The beauty of the sunset seemed to transcend everyday worries for a moment.
His talent for music seems to transcend language barriers and connect with people everywhere.
word-teach:transcend.origin: It is derived from the Latin word transcendere, meaning to climb over or surpass.

check.question: To transcend a limit means to do what?
options: To go beyond or rise above it.
check.why: Transcending means moving past or rising above a specific limitation.

examples: The joy of the vacation felt transient as soon as we had to pack our bags to leave.
The news report discussed the transient nature of fame in the modern digital age.
word-teach:transient.origin: It comes from the Latin word transire, which means to go across or pass by.

check.question: What does it mean if something is transient?
options: It lasts for a very short time.
check.why: Transient describes something that passes quickly or does not last long.

examples: We spent all afternoon arguing over a trivial detail that did not really matter.
The critic felt the movie focused on trivial issues rather than the main plot.
word-teach:trivial.origin: It comes from the Latin word trivialis, meaning belonging to the crossroads or common place.

check.question: How would you describe a trivial matter?
check.why: Trivial things are those that have little significance or value.

examples: The family was unanimous in their decision to order pizza for dinner.
The jury reached a unanimous verdict after several hours of deliberation.
word-teach:unanimous.origin: It is formed from the Latin words unus, meaning one, and animus, meaning mind.

check.question: If a decision is unanimous, what does that mean?
options: Everyone agreed on the same thing.
Only one person made the choice.
There was a lot of disagreement.
check.why: Unanimous means that all members of a group share the same view.

examples: The storm caused unprecedented damage to the small coastal town.
The athlete achieved an unprecedented victory by winning four gold medals in a single day.

check.question: What does it mean to call an event unprecedented?
options: It has happened many times before.
It is a very common occurrence.
check.why: Unprecedented means that something has no prior example or history.

examples: She is such a versatile cook that she can make a delicious meal out of whatever is left in the pantry.
The actor proved his range with a versatile performance that shifted seamlessly from comedy to dark drama.
word-teach:versatile.origin: It derives from the Latin word versatilis, meaning turning or revolving.

check.question: Which of these describes someone who is versatile?
options: Someone who has many different skills
Someone who refuses to change their mind
check.why: Versatile refers to the ability to adapt and perform well in many different areas.

examples: I get a vicarious thrill from hearing about all your adventurous travels around the world.
The audience enjoyed a vicarious sense of victory through the underdog athlete's emotional comeback story.
word-teach:vicarious.origin: It comes from the Latin vicarius, meaning substitute or deputy.

check.question: If you experience something vicariously, how are you experiencing it?
options: Through the actions or experiences of someone else
By doing the activity yourself for the first time
By reading a manual about the activity
check.why: Vicarious experience happens when you feel the emotions or events of another person as if they were your own.

examples: The cost of flights has been so volatile lately that I am waiting to book my vacation.
Analysts are watching the volatile stock market closely as global events continue to cause sudden shifts.

check.question: What does it mean when a price is described as volatile?
options: It is very low and affordable
It is fixed and will never change
check.why: Volatile refers to things that are unstable and prone to frequent or sudden changes.

examples: The garden was filled with whimsical statues that made everyone who walked by smile.
The director is known for her whimsical style, often including magical elements in her live-action films.
word-teach:whimsical.origin: It comes from the noun whim, which is of uncertain origin but likely related to a Scandinavian word for sudden movement.

check.question: Which word best describes something whimsical?
check.why: Whimsical refers to something that is quaint, fanciful, or playfully amusing.

examples: We spent a wholesome afternoon baking cookies and reading stories with the kids.
Critics praised the film for its wholesome message and positive portrayal of family life.
word-teach:wholesome.origin: It is derived from the Middle English word holsum, related to the word whole.

check.question: Which of these would be considered a wholesome activity?
options: Volunteering at a local animal shelter
check.why: Wholesome refers to activities or content that are morally good and promote well-being.

examples: He is a zealous fan who never misses a single game, no matter how far he has to travel.
The author wrote a zealous defense of the local park, hoping to save it from being turned into a parking lot.
word-teach:zealous.origin: It comes from the Greek word zelos, meaning ardor or jealousy.

check.question: How would you describe a zealous person?
check.why: Zealous describes someone who shows intense passion and enthusiasm for a cause or activity.

examples: His laconic reply of just one word made it clear that he was not in the mood to chat.
The detective was known for his laconic style, often solving the mystery with only a few short sentences.
word-teach:laconic.origin: It comes from Lakon, the Greek name for a person from Sparta, who were known for their brief speech.

check.question: What is a laconic person like?
options: They talk for a very long time
check.why: Laconic refers to someone who is brief, concise, and uses as few words as possible.

examples: The benevolent neighbor often leaves fresh vegetables from her garden on our doorstep.
The foundation is known for its benevolent work in providing scholarships to students in need.
word-teach:benevolent.origin: It is from the Latin bene, meaning well, and velle, meaning to wish.

check.question: What does it mean to be benevolent?
check.why: Benevolent describes a person or action that is motivated by the desire to do good for others.

examples: The tension in the room was palpable as we waited for the news.
The athlete's palpable excitement was clear to everyone watching the championship game.

check.question: Which situation describes something that is palpable?
options: A feeling that is easily felt or noticed
A secret that no one knows about
A memory that has been completely forgotten
check.why: Palpable refers to something that is so clear or intense that it feels as if it could be physically touched.

examples: She adopted a cheerful persona to help her feel more confident at the party.
The actor discussed how he struggles to separate his private life from his public persona.
